instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 193 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool compared the draft with essays that students wrote on other assignments. Use its report when you revise:

Tone check against human essay writing (190 words). Distance from the human centre: 1.65 (1.0 is typical for a human text).
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean: 53.19 (per 1,000 words); most human texts are between -18.45 and 31.87. The ending is more upbeat than the rest of the draft by a wider margin than in human writing. Do not close on a lift the body has not earned.
- total charge, positive plus negative: 131.69 (per 1,000 words); most human texts are between 72.62 and 123.86. The draft is more emotionally loaded than human writing of this kind.
- words that carry charge: 32.63 (% of words); most human texts are between 19.18 and 32.19. 
- charge under a negation: 0.0 (% of charge); most human texts are between 0.87 and 10.61. People negate more ('not good', 'isn't fair'). The draft states almost everything in the affirmative.
Inside the human range: positive charge; negative charge; net charge; charge after an intensifier such as 'very'; charge after a contrast word such as 'but'; how unevenly charge is spread over sentences.
These are ranges, not targets. Change wording only where the change also makes the text more specific or more honest.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I am writing to urge you to adopt Policy 1, which would let students bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, as long as they stay off during class.

First, phones matter for safety. Parents want to reach their children when plans change, when someone gets sick, or during an emergency. A complete ban would cut off that connection during the hours families may need it most.

Second, Policy 1 teaches responsibility. Students will soon live in a world where they must decide for themselves when a phone is appropriate. Letting us practice that judgment at school, with clear rules and consequences, prepares us better than simply taking phones away.

Third, a total ban would be hard to enforce. Many students would bring phones anyway and hide them, which creates more conflict between teachers and students. A fair rule that students can follow is more likely to be respected.

Finally, free time is a good moment for checking messages, coordinating rides, or looking up homework details.

Policy 1 keeps classrooms focused while respecting students' needs. I hope you will choose it.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student
